instructions:
You are reading the plain-language text of a codebase map. A reader meets each field ALONE, inside one box, with no paragraph around it, and does not read code.

Judge ONLY these two things:
  1. UNKNOWN WORD — a term the reader has not met and the field does not explain. Product words and words already in the map's Glossary are fine; jargon, an internal codename, or an unexplained abbreviation is not.
  2. LOST PRECISION — the sentence is short and plain but says nothing specific. "The system checks the user" is the shape: grammatical, readable, and it names no decision, no data and no actor. This is the worse failure, because it looks correct.

Do NOT report sentence length, em dashes, code names or an opening "It" — those are counted deterministically and the lead already has the numbers.
Be conservative. Report a field only when you can say WHICH word is unknown, or WHAT the sentence should have said. If in doubt, pass the field.

For each field you flag, return its `where` exactly as given, one of `unknown word` or `lost precision`, and one short line naming the word or the missing specific.

fields.text: Defines every kind of thing a map can hold. Reads a map file back and refuses one whose shape is wrong.
Holds the shared words and formats every other part of the map reads.
Writes a machine-readable description of the map file, for editors and other tools to read.
Merges the pieces each build agent returned into one map. Refuses two pieces that name the same thing twice.
Checks one agent's piece of the map before it is handed in. The agent that made a mistake is the one that fixes it.
Checks that every name in the map points at something real. Also checks that each code link is well formed and really exists.
Checks the use cases, their flows and the happy path against each other. Reports the parts of the code no story covers.
Checks that each business rule names real code lines. Also writes down which files the map says guard access.
Checks how the product connects: its interfaces, its ways in, the services it calls and the processes it runs in.
Checks the saved records, their stores, who owns each data area, and how much of the map was verified.
Routes each typed eval sub-command to the checker that answers it. Loads that checker only when it is asked for.
Reduces one built map to the numbers two builds can be compared on. Two maps of one project never share wording, so counts are what survives.
Judges a fresh map against the accepted one. Returns one word: as good, drifted, or worse.
Folds many doubters' votes and many scorers' marks into one quality report. Never talks to a model itself, so the arithmetic can be tested alone.
Runs one scoring pass end to end and files everything it produced. Can then promote that run to be the accepted baseline.
Finds the relations a rebuild dropped. Re-reads each dropped relation's recorded line to say whether the code still does it.
Moves a project's current map aside so the next build starts from nothing. Moves, never deletes: the old map is what the new one is compared against.
Turns a build's raw chat log into one record per model answer. The log stores one answer as many rows, so counting rows gets every later number wrong.
Reports what one build spent in time and tokens. Divides both by how much map the build produced. Two builds of different sizes then read side by side.
Scores whether the build agent behaved as the method says, one checked rule at a time. Reports numbers, never a pass or a fail.
Refuses a retrospective while the build it would read is still running. A build stamps who made it near the end, so mid-run the stamp still names the previous build.
Asks the code history whether a retrospective's finished rows really shipped. A row saying it is still open while its named change is merged gets proposed again for nothing.
Re-measures every count the tools state about a map that keeps changing. A person writes the sentence twice, so nothing has to guess which sum produced the number.
Plants claims that are false by construction and keeps the answer key. Counts how many of them the doubters caught, which is a number that means something on its own.
Measures how big a project's code is before the map is drawn.
Lets a project declare which of its own code the map must leave out.
Records where every mapped thing belongs, so a rebuild keeps the decision.
Reports how crowded each screen of the map is.
Works out which parts of the map a code change touches.
Bundles a finished map with the conversation that produced it.
Restarts the map server when someone editing the viewer changes its code.
Tells the mapping agent to describe the product before reading code. It orders the goal, the shared words, the people and their goals. The one successful run through those goals comes last.
Says how to list what the product is made of, area by area. Every box gets a plain sentence, a code link and a confidence label. Outside services and the ways in are listed the same way.

Says how to name every place the product meets the outside world. Each place gets one word for what it is, and a side saying whose design it is. It also says how a story crosses one, in both directions.

Says how to write the records the product keeps and the steps of each goal. A step names who acts, on what, and which way the data moves. Machinery shared by several goals is written once and referenced.

Says how to record what runs, what is watched, what is configured and what the product decides. A decision is only worth recording when a product person could have chosen otherwise. Test coverage is measured against the map, never against line counts.

Holds the rules that apply to every part of a build. It says how to write text a reader meets alone, with no page around it. It also sets the order of work, the tools to reach for, and how big one box may be.

Plans the parallel work of a build in three phases. Many agents gather the pieces, one agent merges them, then many agents trace the goals. It says how to size each slice, brief it and wait for the batch.

Plans what happens once every goal has been traced. Fresh agents try to disprove each claim the map makes, against the code. Two more passes write what the product decides and measure what the tests cover.

Runs the closing steps that turn a finished map into a committed one. Corrections land, the record of what was checked is written, then the gates run. It ends by telling the reader where to open the map.
